newsitem.title: GREECE: Greeks pin hopes on Euro court for cheaper cars.
newsitem.headline: Greeks pin hopes on Euro court for cheaper cars.

text.p: Greek consumers have pinned their hopes of cheaper cars on an early court decision against Athens, accused by the European Commission of unequal tax treatment for new and used cars imported from EU countries.
The car taxation issue re-emerged after a Sunday newspaper reported that the finance ministry favoured reducing an unpopular consumption tax on used cars from the EU.
The Sunday Eleftherotypia quoted deputy Finance Minister George Drys as saying it was time to import cheap used cars which were less than three years old from other EU states.
At present, Greece levies extraordinary taxes as high as 400 percent on used cars compared to 75 percent for new cars.
The report enraged car importers who accused the government of being irresponsible because the decision would freeze the car market for months and hurt car-importing companies.
Drys appeared to reverse course on Monday, saying taxes on imported used cars would not be reduced before the end of 1997 or 1998.

"In February, we will go to the European Court where the European Commission has taken us. It will take six to eight months for the final verdict. By the time the decision has been taken, 1997 will be gone," he told state radio.
The European Commission took Greece to the European Court in 1995 for violating EU rules on car taxation. Portugal has faced a similar case.

"We believe the European Court will rule against us but it is preferable to have a drawn out process for fiscal reasons," said a finance ministry official who requested anonymity. "This has been our strategy from the beginning and it has worked."
Greece is struggling to put its public finances in order to meet the Maastricht criteria. Car taxes are expected to reach 150 billion drachmas ($620.6 million) in 1996.
A European Court spokesman said the written procedure on the case finished in April. The next stage is a hearing but this is unlikely to happen before February.
It usually takes six to 10 weeks before the advocate general expresses an opinion and then it can take another two to three months before the final verdict.
Greece is arguing against reducing consumption taxes on used cars to bring them in line with levies on new cars because of environmental concerns.
But Greek consumers did not buy the argument and praised the Commission for taking Greece to court.

"What has the state done for environmental problems in Athens or other cities?" asked Aris Fotopoulos, who works for a private company and wants to buy a used car. "They have suddenly become environmentalists over used cars because they are afraid they will collect less in taxes."
